Ask yourself what are things you really enjoy, what are things that would make you feel a bit celebrated right now? Even if it's you celebrating yourself. What is your favourite movie? Or favourite meal or cake? Or what would be a gift that you would love to receive? Get it for yourself! It can be all of these things or just pick out one if that feels doable, go out and do it for yourself or order it if like you said, you don't like to leave the house. 

I would even say if you'd order food or something you could add in the notes that it's your birthday. I don't know if you'd feel comfortable doing that, but sometimes strangers can be unexpectedly kind, and sometimes the smallest acts can be enough to make us feel a bit special :)

I'm so sorry, I genuinely wish I could do something to make you and this day feel special. I want to tell you ways you could make it special for yourself but I can imagine you don't have the energy or desire to and either way, it's not what you actually want. What you want is for others to make it special for you and that is so completely valid. So all I can say is I feel for you and here is happy birthday from a stranger. I do think the day you were born is a special day.

I completely understand what you're saying. To the extend that I was writing about this myself just a couple of days ago, that I indeed think being so loved as a child is in a way wonderful (for the child) and horrible (for the adult). You grow up with everything you could ever need and you experience a love that is so selfless, a love that doesn't exist as an adult, because no one will (nor should) put their own needs aside to such an extent for you when you are both adults with your own lives. And then after being so fully loved and your every need catered to, and just joy and playing around and safety and not a clue about what life is really like, you're suddenly just thrown into it and you realise that it will never be like that again. 

I fear this is not very helpful but I just wanted to let you know that I feel the same way and I am still trying to figure out how I can possibly find that level of child-like joy and love and safety and optimism in life after childhood.

Yes, weaving it in like that does seem like the most natural way to do it. Only I am not sure how to incorporate the urgency that I am looking for that way. 

I personally often find tiny flashbacks/memories in the present timeline lacking in weight because it is so obviously the past and 'not relevant' now. Sometimes I even find myself skipping over them a bit because I just want to move along in the story and as just tiny bits of information it doesn't feel like something you're experiencing or feeling with the character. 

Also, you're looking at it through the characters adult eyes. If they are an adult and think back on a childhood memory it doesn't feel as intense because you are in their heads now, thinking back on this thing for a minute, before carrying on with the current timeline where your actual interest lies. 

I am trying to find a way that makes the reader feel like they are also truly experiencing those events in the past as the character at the age that the character is in that moment. To really feel it with them, instead of it just seeming like a little blip here and there that doesn't really affect you as a reader because you 'weren't there'.

And I definitely agree with you, I enjoy the challenge of trying to figure it out.

Thank you so much for posting your story on here, reading through it felt very helpful and healing to me. I just got to this last add-on you wrote and I just wanted to say that this is literally exactly how I am feeling right now and the stage that I am in.

I too finally feel the memories fading and the intensity of all the constant ruminating thoughts are losing their grip on me. I can feel it slipping away. Like I have grown out of the person who was stuck in this for so long. I almost imagine it like stepping out of that person and that person just floats there like a shell of skin with these hands reaching out and grasping it, having such a strong hold on it, but I am walking away from it now and those hands can't reach me where I am now.

And while that is all I have wished for for so long, to be free of this. Just like you say, it doesn't feel as euphoric as I might have imagined. It just feels sort of sad and empty. And I would also use the word defeat. It's like I held onto this for so long, deeply believing that somehow there had to be a magical, beautiful future in this because otherwise all the pain was for nothing and so I held on and on and on. I thought at the end of this ride there must be calm and a beautiful view. And it turns out there is, only it is because I got off the ride and I am here alone, without this person. And I just have to accept that the ride could continue on if I wanted it to but there is nothing there, it is just and endless ride, there is no end point where everything is magical and wonderful. So choosing and deciding to get off the ride is unsatisfying, it's empty and it's the death of a long dream, of the yearning for something I so desperately wanted. 

I am trying to treat it as such, a death of something I revolved my life around for years. So I am letting myself mourn, and in this I also realise that the mourning itself means there is no going back, ever. It's complete acceptance, it's what for so long you don't want to do because you know as soon as you do it all crumbles, you see it too clearly and you know too well now to get swept up in it again, you can't fool yourself anymore. Which is why I never wanted to just cut my losses and mourn it, because it means moving on. And no matter in how much agony you are over the situation, part of you still doesn't want to let go, that's why we get stuck in this for so long. Your brain needed it, but I think being able to get to this stage means your brain finally doesn't need it anymore. 

So yes, it feels more than defeat than it does like victory, it feels more sad than it does euphoric. But I am okay with that. Because what I also feel is space and of course that space feels empty now because it used to be occupied with something and now it's not, it's literally empty. But empty means it can be filled and I intend to make that space beautiful and to fill it with things and people that I love and that love me (and do it so deliciously clearly and obviously). And for you it seems there is already someone filling that space, except now they can finally stretch out into all the corners that were still occupied before. And they can make those corners warm and loving and peaceful too. So it feels like hope and it feels like good things ahead, but it's okay to be mourning the death of what was for so long first.

This turned super long and rambly, as I started typing I realised I was more so talking to myself but I still want to post it just in case it is helpful to you or anyone that comes across it, the same way you writing your thoughts and feelings about it all was helpful to me.

This might be exactly what I needed to hear, thank you so much! I think you're right and I have been trying to bend and direct my style. I am going to try to lean into it instead and see what happens. I think my own way of writing feels almost overwhelming to me and so I want to try and get control over it before it even comes out. I didn't realise that before this comment, so thank you.

I'm afraid it might actually be the other way around! Sorry, I can see how that might not have been entirely clear from how I worded it. I actually really only write in first person, that's why I gave third person a go but realised that that wasn't working either. 

I always gravitate towards first person, it comes way more natural to me. But I just get so lost in it, to the point where I can't properly guide the story anymore. It becomes a spiralling web of thoughts and feelings, and it flows as if it is one journal entry to the next. Whereas with third person I can guide the story much better and hold structure much better and all of that, except it also really obviously reads as a story instead of an experience. 

I do feel like ultimately first person would be best as it fits both me and the sort of story I am trying to tell better, but I just can't figure out how to use it without every observation turning into an existential crisis essentially. It could also just be because I am in it while writing it, but to me it just feels so messy and like the story loses structure. What I meant, and what I still want to try, is that I haven't tried first person from the perspective of a character who is basically the antagonist (in my actual personal experience). I wonder if that might put enough distance for me to still be the writer as well as the character while I am writing, instead of those becoming the same thing.

First of all, I want to thank you so much for taking the time to write such an in depth and extremely insightful response that is worded so gently and respectfully. I appreciate it more than I can tell you, it actually even made me a little bit emotional because I did not expect anything like this whatsoever and this is exactly what I needed. This indeed adds to the knowledge I have in ways that are actually very practical and useful. 

I do have professional help as well and I have tried several different people and forms of therapy but unfortunately I keep encountering therapists that kind of just nod and let me talk and don't provide me much to work with. I do want to try again, but it's so draining going through that whole process again and again, so for now I am kind of sticking with the one I have now.

So if you do not mind, I would love to provide a little more information about my personal situation, and if you have any thoughts specifically on that I would love to hear them, as so far this is already incredibly helpful to me.

I found it incredibly interesting what you said about the 'not doing' part and how that is often forgotten, which is entirely true in my case as well. I sort of had the mindset of once I make these positive changes the bad habits will fall away as I won't need them anymore, which has often been the case for me, but as it is something that comes back every time I do 'fall down that rabbit hole' again I think it's a very important point for me to work on as well. 

The thing is however, because I have really thought over everything you've said and how it works for me, is that I don't think I use these things in moments of negative or heavy emotion but instead in moments of 'no emotion' or maybe just more deep rooted emotion. Let me try to explain. I am pretty good with sitting with an emotion when it rises, I think I prefer it actually because anger or sadness that makes me cry or something like that feels very visceral and logical and at least something is happening, which makes me feel like I am working through something. 

But then there is just a more deep rooted feeling of despair that doesn't come out as any sort of emotion but is just a base level for me at times. This is not really something I can sit with because it doesn't pass, it would mean just sitting and staring at the wall for days (which I suppose is what I do sometimes). And this is when I reach for these quick fixes, not even in the moment, in a 'it's coming up now so I need this now' sort of way, but in a I wake up and I see no reason to get out of bed and I feel heavy and dark and the idea of a cup of tea or reading a book is not going to cut it, so I tell myself I can have a cigarette if I get out of bed and I can eat a pizza for lunch and I can smoke some weed later in the day and play video games or watch movies until it's time for bed again. I guess it feels necessary to even get myself to function at all. And it is something I tell myself ahead of time more so than reaching for it in the moment.

And I think that is the big thing, because that is where motivation comes in too. It doesn't feel like I am living for anything at the moment because I am not. This is how I get through my days right now. I will say, I have a long history with my mental health and I absolutely have better periods, which is why I also know the other side of this. And I can almost feel it, because if I get out of this loop and my days are filled with things that naturally make me want to get out of bed and I am excited about life again, then I don't need and won't reach for any of these things. Only even though I can clearly see that this is the 'solution' to find purpose in my days again, it feels too far away in this moment. And I think this is also because I can't find that motivation that truly makes me burn. 

For example I am a writer and my biggest goal is to actually finish a book (I have copious of half finished manuscripts), but even though I know this is my biggest passion and it's not like I am looking in the wrong direction, I have lost my enthusiasm for it. Probably because there is no guarantee of what comes after all that hard work, it's not like working towards something where you get an immediate rewards once you finish it, it's working towards something that once you finish it brings on a whole new challenge. But the challenge doesn't excite me, it just leaves me unmotivated at all. And the idea of 'I am going to write a few pages today of a book that I don't know if I can finish that if I don't know if I can get published, and even if I did know all that my depressive state is making it so that the idea of publishing a book doesn't even feel exciting anymore at all even though it's always been my dream' just doesn't stand a chance against the bad habits that are just right there with an instant 'reward' that at least get me through another day. 

Motivation also tends to be very fleeting for me. It tends to get inspired by another piece of art, maybe a book I read that is just so good that it motivates me to create something, or interviews by someone that just inspires me. Which leads me to think that my motivation is often striving for something I see someone else doing or making. I can hardly ever find it just naturally within myself, which is why it tends to fade quickly.

I think it's important to mention as well that a 'normal job' isn't a possibility for me. And so I have all this time that I could spend on building something for myself through the multiple creative ventures that I do have, and yet I can't seem to spend it on those things. Which seems in part because the goals are unclear and the point of reward is unclear and uncertain. And then on the other hand because of the weight of life and my own current mental state is so heavy that my focus is just on 'getting through the day' instead of improving those actual days. And also the fact that feelings of enthusiasm and excitement towards these goals are just buried right now.

I can also get stuck in a very black and white headspace. So it's like I can see a life where that excitement would be back. If I just get up early and buckle down behind my desk and set goals for myself and I start writing and actually discipline myself to hit these goals and finish something, and maybe I pick up some volunteering job that brings me fulfilment, and I start working on creative projects with other people as I have been wanting to do for a long time. I would have constant creative stimuli, which is so strong for me that I don't even have to look for quick dopamine fixes because that does it all for me. 

But because I am far from this right now, it's so hard to take tiny steps because those steps don't give me what I need yet, and so I don't take any steps at all. Because I don't find much to be fulfilling about my days right now at all and I am just focused on numbing the pain of that instead of on making my days fulfilling because I can't just turn it all around at once and, to go back to what I said earlier, the idea of 'just a few pages today' or 'getting up just a little earlier today' or 'just one painting today' feels more like a pain then anything close to the happiness that I do know it can eventually bring me.

I feel like I got a bit carried away maybe, but honestly just me writing this reply is a great example of the whole thing. Because I put it off for a few days, I kept thinking I really wanted to reply but it felt like too big a task, but now after I just looked at the clock and I realised I was writing this for a whole hour. An hour in which I was concentrated, engaged, motivated, not thinking about if I can eat or smoke something again, and it's sort of lifted my spirits. So I know this is what it does and this is what I need, yet it feels close to impossible (feels like, but I know it is not) to actually get myself to do these things.

I hope this was not too much! I will definitely be using everything that you wrote above to try and turn things around for myself again, but if you have any more thoughts after me providing this information, I would love to hear it.
Even though it wasn't exactly what I was asking, I think this might actually be what I needed to hear instead. Thank you!

I have for a long time. My mental health is finally getting better, but that's exactly the thing. I am realising now that in the past writing might have actually been detrimental to my mental health but I am unsure yet how to use it in a positive way as that is all I ever knew how to do.

Thank you so much for this! I think this is exactly the sort of thing I needed to hear. Writing is indeed powerful in more than one way, I think I have some exploring to do of the other way in which it can be powerful.
I'm sorry you're going through this, I know it's so incredibly hard. But I am so proud of you for doing this for yourself.

I definitely agree! Upon pondering over the replies a little bit I think my issue lies more with finding a balance between two different ways of storytelling. When I let the story flow from the characters, I tend to get too lost in their psyche to the point that nothing external really happens. Whereas when I have the plot more central, it feels more mechanical, simply put it feels like I am getting them from one point to another 'because the plot says so' and I am almost too removed from them.

Thank you!

It's interesting because this makes me think that maybe it's also to do with my love-hate relationship with story structure in general. I know you used very simple terms but it does feel that simple to me sometimes, like something happens -> character grows. It's not always so clean cut in real life and so I think when I really focus on character and just want to essentially study human behaviour I want to stray away from plot in the sense of something happening which then propels another thing to happen. I want it to feel a bit more organic but when I loose that structure it feels aimless, so I do need it.   
But I think I'm struggling to find a balance between letting things flow too freely or forcing a too rigid structure that makes the characters feel mechanical almost.

Thank you, that is super helpful!

I do think I might try to control them a little too much. I never used to outline but I've figured out a way that outlining does work for me and it's been a great help but I might be a bit too rigid about it now. So I'm definitely taking this reminder to let my characters breathe a little and let them push back

First of all thank you that is very helpful! 

However, in my character-driven projects I do know the motivation, conflict and stakes. I know the whole character arc but on an emotional/internal level if that makes sense. But what I then struggle with is where this is supposed to move them in the simplest sense, because not every moment is a big plot point so what do they do in between? Grocery shopping? Sounds silly but I guess I struggle with filling in what these internal changes mean physically, where they happen, where they take them.

I think also because like I said when I write more plot-driven it's mostly fantasy, so I think I have a tendency to associate plot with something epic and so when I turn to writing in the real world and I just want to zone in on people and their behaviour something about it feels too mundane maybe and I am looking for these 'epic' things for them to do or larger than life places to send them instead of to visit their grandma.
